status: Research input, not yet reviewed by a person and not wired into the builder.
units: EUR bn nominal unless stated; USD at ECB yearly averages (2019 1.1195, 2020 1.1422, 2021 1.1827, 2022 1.053, 2023 1.0813, 2024 1.0824, 2025 1.13, 2026 1.162). 2026 = January-August, not annualised (as in laundered_r6.json). "Russian crude in fuel" levels are the money Russia was paid for the crude inside the fuel (fuel value x Russian share x crude content), the same concept as laund.years in site/data.json. "Gain to Russia" is the change-view part (the site's laund part, sign flipped: positive = Russia gained), cumulative 2022-2026, worked out with the site's own model (site/index.html calc()) on a patched copy of site/data.json.
question: How much of the fuel that third countries buy from refining hubs embodies Russian crude, who bears Russia's gain on it, and what evidence-based central rule should replace "laundered oil not counted" as an alternative.

rule_proposal.owner_decision: "What has evidence should be counted as such, then on top we can add speculative." Central = the evidence-based share; speculative versions only as range ends / method band.

central_measured_content.rule: Russian crude in the fuel a buyer imported = sum over origins of the buyer's own customs imports of HS 2710 from that origin (supplier export records x1.05 where the buyer does not report, or where the buyer records a trading hub as consignor) x the measured Russian share of that origin's refinery or hub pool that year x crude content (crude_content.json). Pre-war level measured the same way (2019-2021), so the change compares like with like and no route rule is needed. Counted at Russia's net gain on crude, both ways, in volumes (laundered_volumes(), unchanged).
central_measured_content.russian_share_of_origin_pool: Refiner countries: customs crude imports from Russia / all crude imports, tonnes (UN Comtrade, the refiner's own report): India 1.3% (2019), 2.1% (2021), 15.2% (2022), 37.8% (2023), 38.1% (2024), 33.7% (2025), 30% (2026, KSE/CREA refinery data: 21-27% of Indian exports Nov 2025-Apr 2026, Jamnagar 38% May-Jul 2026, Vadinar 100%); China 15.4-15.7% pre-war, 16.0-19.2% after; Türkiye ~15-20% pre-war, 35-54% after. Trading hubs (Singapore, Malaysia, Oman): mass balance of the hub's own customs, crude feed plus product imports by origin x each origin's share. EU refiners 27% pre-war (EU crude from Russia), ~2% from 2023. UAE: CREA Russian products / UAE product exports (as in energy.json).
central_measured_content.option_A_recommended: Only refiners whose own payments to Russia the builder already nets off (India, China, Türkiye, UAE, Brunei, EU refiners) pass Russian crude to buyers; Korea, Japan, Thailand, Taiwan and the hubs' own refineries keep theirs (their own to_rus already holds it). Consistent with "refiners counted once" without touching other countries' payments.
central_measured_content.option_B_not_recommended_now: All refiners pass it on (Korea 6.1-6.4% Russian crude in 2019-2021, 0% from 2023; Japan 3.6-5.4% -> 0%; Thailand 3-6% -> 0%; Singapore/Malaysia own crude 1.5-11% -> 0%). This is the fuller physical picture but needs the builder to take the passed-on part off Korea's, Japan's, Thailand's, Singapore's and Malaysia's own payments to Russia, base years included; otherwise their pre-war cut is credited twice (to them and to their buyers). Shown per buyer as option_B.
central_measured_content.why_this_is_evidence: Every input is a published measurement: buyer customs by origin, refiner customs by crude origin, Kpler-based refinery slates (CREA, KSE). "Perfect mixing" (a refinery's Russian share applies to all its products) is the convention CREA, KSE Institute and Australian sanctions guidance use; KSE notes it is "indicative ... rather than a precise molecular tracing assessment". It does not assume who bears the gain beyond the project's existing premise (the buyer of the fuel is charged as if it bought the crude).

speculative_low_method_band.rule: Only half of Russia's gain on the measured crude is charged to the fuel buyer: the redirected-trade incidence already used for "paid" (attrib; world ratio about 0.5 for buyers who bought more). Rationale: crude is fungible; Babina et al. (CEPR DP17957) find Russia redirected its crude to India, China and Türkiye at a discount, so a single fuel buyer's demand moves Russia's revenue by less than the full embodied crude. "Not counted" (zero) contradicts the measured content and is dropped from the band.
speculative_low_method_band.effect_all_161_countries: Replacing laund_off by laund_half with the current series changes 2 groups: Mauritius and Nepal from leaning Russia to certain Russia (as the round-39 certainty audit predicted). Nothing else changes group.

speculative_high_method_band.key: laund_model (for buyers given a measured series) / laund_route (unchanged, elsewhere)
speculative_high_method_band.rule: The current hub-chain model (refiner exports to the destination x country-average share x 0.699, passed on by hub resale shares, pre-war base from round4a laundered_prewar) kept as the alternative. For buyers with a measured series both routes are measured by their own customs, so the route rule has nothing to hold; laund_route is dropped for them.

rule_proposal.range: Low/high of the measured series combine the origin share band (India x0.75/x1.27, China/Türkiye +-20%, UAE +-50%, hubs from their inputs' bands), crude content low/high (crude_content.json), and +-10% quantity (+-20% where from mirrors or carried). The pre-war base gets the same band.
rule_proposal.structural_label: Like Nigeria/Dangote: where a buyer's own refinery closed for reasons unrelated to the war (New Zealand: Marsden Point, 31 March 2022, decided in 2021; South Africa: Engen Durban after the December 2020 fire, SAPREF paused end-March 2022), its fuel imports rose 1.7-2.7 times. The rise in Russian crude bought through them is partly that closure. Proposed: label it structural (value kept), and show the variant with the pre-war base scaled to post-closure imports (structural_variant per buyer).

key_findings: For Pacific buyers supplied through Singapore (Fiji, New Caledonia, Papua New Guinea, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Vanuatu) the measured Russian-derived share of the Singapore pool is 3.0% pre-war and 3.2-3.9% in 2022-2026 (option A); Malaysia 2.5% -> 3.5-4.5%. The current model has the content rising about 2.7 times. Measured, Fiji's change is -0.015 bn (Russia gains 0.015) with a range 0.000-0.034, against 0.012 (-0.003 to 0.044) now: the range no longer crosses zero, but only just.

Korea, the largest supplier of New Zealand, Australia, the Philippines and Chile, bought 6.1-6.4% of its crude from Russia in 2019-2021 and none from 2023 to 2025 (Korean customs). Japan and Thailand the same. Under option B buyers of Korean fuel get credit; under option A that credit stays with Korea.

China's Russian crude share barely moved (15.4-15.7% pre-war, 16.0-19.2% after). Buyers of Chinese fuel (Philippines, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Chile) see little change in content; their change is volume.

India's moved from 1.3-2.1% to 34-38%: Nepal (all Indian Oil Corporation fuel), Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, South Africa, Mauritius, Tanzania, Kenya are where the measured rise is real. Nepal: Russia gains 0.88 bn (0.39-1.41), up from 0.66 now; becomes certain (towards Russia) once laund_off is replaced.

India's export records charge East African transit hubs with fuel that goes on to landlocked neighbours: India records USD 2.2-3.0 bn a year to Tanzania (FY2022-26) against Tanzania's own 0.66-0.91 bn, and 0.6-1.8 bn to Mozambique against 0.07-0.2 bn. Using the buyer's own (home-use) customs cuts Tanzania's gain to Russia from 1.17 to 0.51 bn and Mozambique's from 0.34 to 0.12 bn; the difference belongs to Zambia, DRC, Malawi, Zimbabwe, Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda (not yet computed).

Pre-war Russian crude in fuel was larger than round4a.json's laundered_prewar for Asian buyers (it counted China mainly), because Korea, Japan, Thailand, Malaysia and EU refiners all ran some Russian crude. Measured both ways (option A), the pre-war base is 1.6 times the current one for the Philippines, 1.7 for Fiji, 2.0 for Chile and 2.2 for Bangladesh; New Zealand's is about the same.

quotes.text: The analysis applies a perfect-mixing refinery attribution methodology ... if 40% of a refinery's crude oil intake originates from Russia, it is assumed that 40% of the refinery's exported refined products are derived from Russian crude oil.
products derived from Russian crude accounted for approximately 21% of total exports in P1 2026, significantly below past levels of 48% in P1 2025 and 27% in P4 2025.
the share of exports destined for non-sanctioning countries increased from 73% to 87% for total exports and from 74% to 89% for exports derived from Russian crude oil.

G7+ countries imported EUR 14.7 bn (25.7 mn tonnes) of oil products from refineries using Russian crude ... An estimated EUR 7.2 bn (12.5 mn tonnes) of these oil product imports were estimated to have been refined from Russian crude.

Australia remained the single largest importer among sanctioning countries, purchasing a total of EUR 3.4 bn of oil products from refineries using Russian crude. An estimated EUR 1.6 bn of their imports were refined from Russian crude.

Refineries in India, Türkiye, Brunei and Georgia that use Russian crude exported EUR 510 mn of oil products to sanctioning countries in August [2026] ... About EUR 189 mn of these products were estimated to be refined from Russian crude. Vadinar took 100% of its crude from Russia in the first eight months of 2026, up from 81% in 2025.

nearly $100 million [NZD] worth of fuel refined from Russian crude arrived here in the past year ... around 75,000 tonnes of the fuel imported to New Zealand was produced using Russian crude ... roughly $70 million in tax revenue for the Kremlin.
China (57.7 million tonnes), India ... and Singapore (0.5 million tonnes) increased imports of Russian crude oil
Russia was able to divert crude oil exports from Europe to substitute markets like India, China, and Turkey ... The crude oil discounts were not as significant as those indicated in Urals prices.

Not covered here: the EU, USA, UK and Australia (laundered_eu.json / laundered_r6.json are customs- or CREA-refinery-based already), and the landlocked East/Southern African buyers that receive transit fuel.

open_questions: Option A vs B: should Korea, Japan, Thailand, Singapore and Malaysia be treated as refiners that pass Russian crude on (B, fuller, needs their deductions) or keep it (A)? B moves Fiji, New Caledonia and the Solomon Islands to the Ukraine side (their suppliers stopped buying Russian crude) and the Philippines to certain.

Indian Oil Corporation's refinery-level Russian share (Barauni, Haldia, Paradip supply Nepal): Paradip was 7-29% in 2025-26 per KSE, below the national 34%; a Kpler pull per IOC refinery would narrow Nepal.
Transit fuel through Tanzania, Mozambique and Kenya: assign India's and the UAE's records above home use to Zambia, DRC, Malawi, Zimbabwe, Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda from their own customs.

UAE share (Russian products relabelled from Fujairah, 15% in 2022 to 3.5% in 2025) is the weakest input and drives Pakistan, Kenya, Mauritius and the Maldives; a Kpler UAE re-export split would settle it.
Cameroon records India as origin for fuel India does not record (origin vs consignment through Togo/Europe); no Cameroonian customs after 2023 in Comtrade.
Structural label for New Zealand and South Africa (refinery closures): owner decision.
Bangladesh and New Caledonia have no own customs in Comtrade; Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation import records by origin would replace the mirrors.
